notes: Sample telegram_support_commands.json - what the bot will do when somebody types a command. Copy to telegram_support_commands.json and edit.

'command_type' is the clearance the command demands. A person may run it only when their telegram_users.json 'user_type' is at least this number, AND the chat's 'allow_command' is at least this number too. Both gates, every time.

This file says WHO may ask. data/emergency_operations.json says HOW HARD it is to confirm once asked - the two carry the same number for the same operation and are deliberately separate files, because they answer different questions and the shared operations layer reads no Telegram settings at all.

'is_group' / 'is_private' decide where a command is accepted. Anything that changes a production system should be private only: a group message is seen by everyone in it and answered by whoever types first.
'action_type' picks the handler. 'cli_execute' runs a module CLI as a child process; the named handlers ('list_server_id', 'list_all_command', ...) answer from the store without starting anything.

In 'command_argv', {python}, {config_path} and every declared parameter name are substituted before the process starts. Values are substituted as data, and a parameter with a 'validator' is checked first - a free-text value reaching a shell or a SQL statement unchecked is the failure this shape exists to prevent.
'requires_secret_key' passes the decryption passphrase to the child process, which anything touching a database needs and a pure listing does not.
'node_role' limits a command to the node that can actually serve it, so a command scheduled on a machine with no access to the estate is never offered there.

telegram_support_commands._note: The simplest possible entry: a fixed reply, no action. command_type 0 means anyone the bot knows may use it.
A named handler. It answers from the store, so it starts no process and needs no secret key. {result_listing} is filled in by the handler.
Lists the server_id values every other command takes as an argument. Worth keeping at a low clearance: without it nobody can use the commands that need one.

telegram_support_commands._note: Attach an .xlsx or a delimited text file (.txt/.csv/.tsv, incl. a block pasted out of Excel) and get a queryable table; the format is detected from the file's bytes, not its name. Private-only (is_private 1 / is_group 0): it writes to a real database, and a group chat is the wrong place for a command whose effect nobody else in the room can see. if_exists stays at the module default of 'error' rather than being pinned to 'drop' here - a Telegram user must not be able to destroy an existing table by re-sending a file. table_name is not prompted for; blank means temp_<random>, and the generated name is in the reply. action_config._note_timeout: 24h, and it is a BACKSTOP, not the task's deadline. The background-task poller SIGKILLs the runner at this age (command_processor.check_cli_background_tasks), so whatever stands here silently caps every SQL task started from Telegram no matter what sql_targets.json says - at the old 7200 a 6-file folder task of ~2h per file was killed during file 2, mid-statement. The real per-task bound is time_window.timeout on the sql_target, which is both the statement timeout per file and the stale-run threshold. tests/test_telegram_run_sql_task_command.py pins this value at or above every configured target timeout so raising a target's timeout past the Telegram ceiling fails the suite instead of getting the task killed in production.

conditional_args._note: Conditional, exactly like remote_password_text below. It used to sit in command_argv unconditionally, so `password_text = -` (the skip sentinel, meaning 'reuse the ref') still handed the CLI an env var holding the literal '-'. That stored a password of '-' when the ref was new, and refused with 'already exists with a different value' when it was not - the reuse path could never be reached.

parameters.validation_error: answer yes or no
parameters.prompt_text:
If an instance with that name already exists, recreate it? yes / no
yes = DESTROYS the existing containers AND their data volumes, then rebuilds from scratch (and replaces the stored password for that ref). Answer no unless you mean it — an existing instance is never touched otherwise.

parameters.name: install_docker
parameters.validation_error: answer yes or no
parameters.prompt_text:

yes = SSH in and install Docker (needs the SSH user to have sudo), add it to the docker group, create the containers dir. Use yes for a fresh Ubuntu VM. Answer no for deploy_target=worker or a VM that already has Docker.

action_config._note: Who is holding an open transaction on SALESDB (192.0.2.115). Reads only - it runs through common.cli trace-session, which goes through sql_run and always rolls back, so this command cannot change anything and needs no confirm step (unlike spbot_kill_spid). Pinned to 70-115/SALESDB because that is the instance the blocking incidents are on (audits/20260811_audit_ax_long_open_transactions_70_115.md); a second entry can be added for another target rather than making the operator type a server_id every time. session_id 0 means 'scan everything older than min_tran_seconds' - the common case, so it is the default and the argument is optional. The `defaults` entry is what makes the no-argument form work: an optional argument that was not typed keeps its default instead of being blanked (fixed 2026-08-12 in command_processor.cli_action_values, after this command failed in production with 'request is not valid JSON').
